The Barred forest falcon (Micrastur ruficollis) hatches from eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] after a developmental period of 34 days [ab = 34 days]. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the altricial nestling is remarkably low, averaging just 28 grams [Ww0 = 28 grams], a value that underscores the substantial energetic investment required to provision the growing chick. This initial mass is consistent with the pattern observed in other small- to medium-sized forest falcons, where parental provisioning commences immediately upon hatching. The chick remains in the nest, dependent on the adults for food and thermoregulation, for a period of approximately 38 days after hatching [tx = approximately 38 days after hatching], at which point it achieves fledging under typical thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This milestone marks the transition from a stationary, parental-fed nestling to a mobile fledgling, capable of short flights but still reliant on the parents for several additional weeks.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 261 grams [Wwi = 261 grams] and males achieving a substantially smaller ultimate wet weight of 164 grams [Wwi = 164 grams]. The range of variation recorded among adult females spans from approximately 200 to 322 grams, while males typically range between 144 and 184 grams, reflecting the broader size variation that can occur within populations. This dimorphism is common among raptors and is thought to facilitate niche partitioning during the breeding season, allowing the larger female to remain on the nest for extended periods while the smaller, more agile male undertakes the majority of hunting. These asymptotic values represent the maximum attained body masses in healthy, reproductively active adults, as confirmed by field measurements from Neotropical populations throughout the species' range.

Under the same thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] that characterize the active metabolic state of this species, the Barred forest falcon attains sexual maturity at 114 days after hatching [tp = 114 days after hatching]. This is a relatively rapid progression to puberty compared to many larger forest raptors, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction in a competitive tropical environment. Following the onset of gonadal maturation, the time since birth at first brood is approximately 694 days [tR = approximately 694 days], or about 1.9 years, measured at the same ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delay between reaching puberty and initiating a first successful breeding attempt is likely driven by the need to acquire a suitable territory and a mate, as well as to develop the hunting proficiency required to provision offspring.

Reproductive output in the Barred forest falcon is modest but typical of forest-dwelling accipitrids. Females lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], and typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive rate, when expressed over the species' documented maximum lifespan of approximately 13.3 years [am = approximately 13.3 years] — again observed at 40 °C [T = 40 °C] — suggests that a female may produce between 26 and 40 eggs over the course of her lifetime, depending on the success of each nesting attempt. The clutch size of two to three eggs is conservative relative to many open-country raptors, a pattern often associated with the constraints of provisioning young in a structurally complex forest habitat where prey detection and capture are more challenging.

Basal metabolic rate, measured as resting oxygen consumption under thermoneutral conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], averages 130.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 130.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is relatively modest for a raptor of this body size, reflecting the energetic adaptations of an ambush predator that relies on short bursts of activity rather than sustained pursuit. The maximum longevity of approximately 13.3 years [am = approximately 13.3 years] places this species among the longer-lived Neotropical raptors of its size, a longevity that is consistent with its relatively low basal metabolic rate and modest reproductive output, reinforcing the slow life-history strategy inferred from these demographic parameters at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The combination of a low metabolic demand, moderate lifespan, and limited annual fecundity suggests that population turnover is low, making the Barred forest falcon potentially vulnerable to habitat fragmentation that reduces both nesting sites and prey availability across its Neotropical range.
